stories.title: RSPB reports record-breaking chough numbers
stories.summary: A record-breaking number of choughs have made their nests around the Cornish coastline this summer proving the breed is in "robust health", a bird conservation charity has said. RSPB England said 161 choughs had been counted in Cornwall - 32 more than the 129 recorded in 2025. The charity said the new birds came from 56 successful breeding pairs meaning the average productivity of a Cornish chough nest was three fledglings. It said choughs died out in Cornwall in the 1970s but returned in 2001 when three birds believed to be from Ireland landed at Lizard Point and began the rebreeding of the population. Peter Hall, a National Trust chough monitoring volunteer on the Lizard, is on his 11th year of monitoring the nest sites. He said he had not foreseen a time when he would be monitoring so many sites and "certainly not having 16 choughlets fledge". Hall said: "The past two winters we have been blessed with chatterings in excess of 20 chough around the Lizard - a far cry from the solitary single pair we had when I started as part of the then nest protection team in 2016. "Long may the successful return of this iconic Cornish bird delight myself and others." The charity said the Lizard was the prime breeding ground for the Cornish chough with 26 chicks, 11 more than 2025, emerging from eight nests on the peninsula. National Trust volunteer Lydia Allt said 2026 had been "an exceptional one" for choughs on the Lizard and across Cornwall. She said: "Thanks to a quarter of a century of conservation work, partnership working and the support of local farmers and land managers, we are seeing record numbers ofchough across the area. "Their remarkable recovery shows what can be achieved when habitats are restored and protected, giving wildlife the space it needs to thrive.

stories.title: Heavy periods study to create world's largest biobank
stories.summary: A major new research project aiming to transform care for women with heavy periods is to create the world's largest menstrual fluid biobank. The CycleTrack study hopes to improve understanding of heavy menstrual bleeding and related conditions such as endometriosis and fibroids, helping speed up diagnosis and treatment for millions of women. Led by researchers from the universities of Bristol and Exeter, it will collect real-time health data and menstrual fluid samples from thousands of women across the UK. Professor Gemma Sharp said the study was going to be "a real game changer" for menstrual health research and could cut waiting times for effective treatment. As part of the study, researchers are working with women who have personal experience of heavy periods. Maria Lewis, 34, from Weston-super-Mare, has lived with heavy menstrual bleeding since she first started menstruating and was diagnosed with endometriosis last year. She has taken part in the Children of the 90s, external study since childhood and was keen to support the latest research. Describing the impact of her condition, she said: "It's horrific. I'm in pain every day." Although she cannot take part in the menstrual fluid collection because she takes hormonal contraception to manage her symptoms and no longer menstruates, she believes the research could help improve understanding of conditions affecting women. She said: "Absolutely, it needs more of a platform and a louder voice." Heavy menstrual bleeding, sometimes known as HMB, affects up to half of women worldwide and can have a significant impact on physical, emotional and social wellbeing.

stories.title: No formaldehyde detected in Chinese cabbage shipments to South Korea so far, say authorities
stories.summary: There were allegations that some agricultural produce buyers in China had dipped cabbage in a formaldehyde solution.
article_sentences: The South Korean food safety authorities said on Aug 26 that they had found no detectable formaldehyde in eight shipments of Chinese cabbage tested since reports emerged that the chemical had been used to preserve cabbage in parts of China.
The Ministry of Food and Drug Safety said the eight shipments, which were reported for import on Aug 24 and Aug 25, all tested negative for formaldehyde.
The ministry began testing Chinese cabbage imports more extensively on Aug 24 following reports about the use of formaldehyde.
Under the strengthened measures, every shipment of cabbage imported from China is being tested for the chemical during customs clearance, the ministry said.
The authorities are also testing Chinese-made kimchi and pickled cabbage by manufacturer.
The ministry said it plans to collect and test products from all Chinese manufacturers, including cabbage, kimchi and pickled cabbage already being sold in South Korea.
Results will be released as testing is completed.
The measures follow a video posted online alleging that some agricultural produce buyers in China had dipped cabbage in a formaldehyde solution before loading it for transportation.
The scope of the reported practice and whether any such products entered.
South Korea have not been established.
The issue has attracted widespread public attention in South Korea, as China accounts for about 99 per cent of the country’s imported kimchi.
According to data from Korea Customs Service, South Korea imported a record 336,221 tonnes of kimchi from China in 2025, the highest annual volume on record.

stories.title: Next Atlantic tropical storm will be named Dolly but no connection to Parton's death
stories.summary: Storm systems are named by procedures set by the World Meteorological Organisation and the lists of names are reused every six years.
article_sentences: Storm systems are named by procedures set by the World Meteorological Organisation and the lists of names are reused every six years.

The next tropical storm that develops in the Atlantic this hurricane season will be named Dolly, but the timing is pure coincidence and has no connection to country music star Dolly Parton’s death on Tuesday.
For the Atlantic region, the lists are alphabetical and alternate between male and female names.
This season started with Tropical Storm Arthur coming ashore on the US Gulf Coast in June, and Tropical Storm Bertha dumped rain in Louisiana and Texas in July.
Tropical Storm Cristobal formed and quickly dissipated in the Atlantic earlier in August.
The National Hurricane Centre was monitoring a weather system off Africa that may strengthen into a named tropical storm.

Conditions were favourable for the area of thunderstorms south of the Cabo Verde Islands to become a tropical depression sometime in the next week, forecasters at the Miami-based centre said on Tuesday evening.
If it further develops, with maximum sustained winds of at least 63 kph, the system would be named Tropical Storm Dolly.
Forecasters said another weather system in the Atlantic far northeast of Bermuda was disorganized Tuesday and had a poor chance of further development.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has forecast a below-average Atlantic hurricane season due to the El Niño climate phenomenon.
It forecast eight to 14 named storms, with three to six of them reaching hurricane strength and one to three of those intensifying to major hurricanes.
The NHC and other weather agencies name storms to easily communicate warnings about them to people and to avoid confusion.
